blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Foreword

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The National Curriculum Framework 2005, recommends that children’s life at school
must be linked to their life outside the school. This principle marks a departure from
the legacy of bookish learning which continues to shape our system and causes a
gap between the school, home and community. The syllabi and textbooks developed
on the basis of NCF signify an attempt to implement this basic idea. They also
attempt to discourage rote learning and the maintenance of sharp boundaries between
different subject areas. We hope these measures will take us significantly further in
the direction of a child-centred system of education outlined in the National Policy
on Education (1986).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The success of this effort depends on the steps that school principals and teachers
will take to encourage children to reflect on their own learning and to pursue
imaginative activities and questions. We must recognise that, given space, time and
freedom, children generate new knowledge by engaging with the information passed
on to them by adults. Treating the prescribed textbook as the sole basis of examination
is one of the key reasons why other resources and sites of learning are ignored.
Inculcating creativity and initiative is possible if we perceive and treat children as
participants in learning, not as receivers of a fixed body of knowledge.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
These aims imply considerable change in school routines and mode of functioning.
Flexibility in the daily time-table is as necessary as rigour in implementing the annual
calendar so that the required number of teaching days are actually devoted to teaching.
The methods used for teaching and evaluation will also determine how effective this
textbook proves for making children’s life at school a happy experience, rather than
a source of stress or boredom. Syllabus designers have tried to address the problem
of curricular burden by restructuring and reorienting knowledge at different stages
with greater consideration for child psychology and the time available for teaching.
The textbook attempts to enhance this endeavour by giving higher priority and space
to opportunities for contemplation and wondering, discussion in small groups, and
activities requiring hands-on experience.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Rationalisation of Content in the Textbooks

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In view of the COVID-19 pandemic, it is imperative to reduce content load on
students. The National Education Policy 2020, also emphasises reducing the content
load and providing opportunities for experiential learning with creative mindset. In
this background, the NCERT has undertaken the exercise to rationalise the textbooks
across all classes. Learning Outcomes already developed by the NCERT across
classes have been taken into consideration in this exercise.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Contents of the textbooks have been rationalised in view of the following:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
• Overlapping with similar content included in other subject areas in the same
class

• Similar content included in the lower or higher class in the same subject

• Difficulty level

• Content, which is easily accessible to students without much interventions from
teachers and can be learned by children through self-learning or peer-learning

• Content, which is irrelevant in the present context

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This present edition, is a reformatted version after carrying out the changes
given above.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Preface

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Through the years, from the time of the Kothari Commission, there have been
several committees looking at ways of making the school curriculum meaningful
and enjoyable for the learners. Based on the understanding developed over the
years, a National Curriculum Framework (NCF) was finalised in 2005. As part of
this exercise, a National Focus Group on Teaching of Mathematics was formed. Its
report, which came in 2005, highlighted a constructivist approach to the teaching
and learning of mathematics.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The essence of this approach is that children already know, and do some
mathematics very naturally in their surroundings, before they even join school. The
syllabus, teaching approach, textbooks etc., should build on this knowledge in a way
that allows children to enjoy mathematics, and to realise that mathematics is more
about a way of reasoning than about mechanically applying formulae and algorithms.
The students and teachers need to perceive mathematics as something natural and
linked to the world around us. While teaching mathematics, the focus should be on
helping children to develop the ability to particularise and generalise, to solve and
pose meaningful problems, to look for patterns and relationships, and to apply the
logical thinking behind mathematical proof. And, all this in an environment that the
children relate to, without overloading them.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This is the philosophy with which the mathematics syllabus from Class I to
Class XII was developed, and which the textbook development committee has tried
to realise in the present textbook. More specifically, while creating the textbook, the
following broad guidelines have been kept in mind.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ The matter needs to be linked to what the child has studied before, and to
her experiences.
$\bullet$ The language used in the book, including that for ‘word problems’, must be
clear, simple and unambiguous.
$\bullet$ Concepts/processes should be introduced through situations from the
children’s environment.
$\bullet$ For each concept/process give several examples and exercises, but not of
the same kind. This ensures that the children use the concept/process again
and again, but in varying contexts. Here ‘several’ should be within reason,
not overloading the child.
$\bullet$ Encourage the children to see, and come out with, diverse solutions to
problems.

blocks.label: Page-number
blocks.text: $$viii$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ As far as possible, give the children motivation for results used.
$\bullet$ All proofs need to be given in a non-didactic manner, allowing the learner to
see the flow of reason. The focus should be on proofs where a short and
clear argument reinforces mathematical thinking and reasoning.
$\bullet$ Whenever possible, more than one proof is to be given.
$\bullet$ Proofs and solutions need to be used as vehicles for helping the learner
develop a clear and logical way of expressing her arguments.
$\bullet$ All geometric constructions should be accompanied by an analysis of the
construction and a proof for the steps taken to do the required construction.
Accordingly, the children would be trained to do the same while doing
constructions.
$\bullet$ Add such small anecdotes, pictures, cartoons and historical remarks at
several places which the children would find interesting.
$\bullet$ Include optional exercises for the more interested learners. These would
not be tested in the examinations.
$\bullet$ Give answers to all exercises, and solutions/hints for those that the children
may require.
$\bullet$ Whenever possible, propagate constitutional values.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you will see while studying this textbook, these points have been kept in mind
by the Textbook Development Committee. The book has particularly been created
with the view to giving children space to explore mathematics and develop the abilities
to reason mathematically. Further, two special appendices have been given — Proofs
in Mathematics, and Mathematical Modelling. These are placed in the book for
interested students to study, and are only optional reading at present. These topics
may be considered for inclusion in the main syllabi in due course of time.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As in the past, this textbook is also a team effort. However, what is unusual
about the team this time is that teachers from different kinds of schools have been
an integral part at each stage of the development. We are also assuming that teachers
will contribute continuously to the process in the classroom by formulating examples
and exercises contextually suited to the children in their particular classrooms. Finally,
we hope that teachers and learners would send comments for improving the textbook
to the NCERT.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS 1

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered
irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We
begin with Section 1.2 namely the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
There are many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers. We
touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF (Highest Common
Factor) or GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) of two positive integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something
with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number
can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way — this important fact is the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and
understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics.
We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic to prove the irrationality of many of
the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ .

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a
product of its prime factors. For instance, $2 = 2$, $4 = 2 \times 2$, $253 = 11 \times 23$, and so on.
Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any
natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Take any collection of prime numbers, say $2, 3, 7, 11$ and $23$. If we multiply
some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish,
we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many).
Let us list a few :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 5313$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 10626$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2^2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 21252$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes.
What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite
number of integers, or infinitely many? Infact, there are infinitely many primes. So,
if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite
collection of primes that is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
collection of numbers, all the
primes and all possible products
of primes. The question is – can
we produce all the composite
numbers this way? What do you
think? Do you think that there
may be a composite number
which is not the product of
powers of primes? Before we
answer this, let us factorise
positive integers, that is, do the
opposite of what we have done
so far.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We are going to use the
factor tree with which you are
all familiar. Let us take some
large number, say, 32760, and
factorise it as shown.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So we have factorised $32760$ as $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of
primes, i.e., $32760 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of powers of primes. Let us try
another number, say, $123456789$. This can be written as $3^2 \times 3803 \times 3607$. Of course,
you have to check that $3803$ and $3607$ are primes! (Try it out for several other natural
numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be
written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and is called
the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** because of its basic crucial importance
to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) :** *Every composite*
*number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation*
*is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.*

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
An equivalent version of Theorem 1.1 was probably
first recorded as Proposition 14 of Book IX in Euclid’s
Elements, before it came to be known as the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. However, the
first correct proof was given by Carl Friedrich Gauss
in his *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*.

Carl Friedrich Gauss is often referred to as the ‘Prince
of Mathematicians’ and is considered one of the three
greatest mathematicians of all time, along with
Archimedes and Newton. He has made fundamental
contributions to both mathematics and science.

Carl Friedrich Gauss
(C.E. 1777 – C.E. 1855)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can
be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any
composite number it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a ‘unique’
way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite
number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as long as we
are not particular about the order in which the primes occur. So, for example, we
regard $2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$ as the same as $3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 2$, or any other possible order in which
these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The prime factorisation of a natural number, greater than $1$, is unique,
except for the order of its factors.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, given a composite number $x$, we factorise it as $x = p_1 p_2 ... p_n$, where
$p_1, p_2, ..., p_n$ are primes and written in ascending order, i.e., $p_1 \le p_2$
$\le ... \le p_n$. If we combine the same primes, we will get powers of primes. For example,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$32760 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number
is factorised, is unique.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within
mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Consider the numbers $4^n$, where $n$ is a natural number. Check whether
there is any value of $n$ for which $4^n$ ends with the digit zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : If the number $4^n$, for any $n$, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be
divisible by 5. That is, the prime factorisation of $4^n$ would contain the prime 5. This is
not possible because $4^n = (2)^{2n}$; so the only prime in the factorisation of $4^n$ is 2. So, the
uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no
other primes in the factorisation of $4^n$. So, there is no natural number $n$ for which $4^n$
ends with the digit zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers
using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it!
This method is also called the prime factorisation method. Let us recall this method
through an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.
Solution : We have : $6 = 2^1 \times 3^1$ and $20 = 2 \times 2 \times 5 = 2^2 \times 5^1$.
You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$, as done in your
earlier classes.
Note that HCF(6, 20) = $2^1$ = **Product of the smallest power of each common**
**prime factor in the numbers.**
LCM (6, 20) = $2^2 \times 3^1 \times 5^1$ = **Product of the greatest power of each prime factor,**
**involved in the numbers.**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the example above, you might have noticed that HCF$(6, 20) \times \text{LCM}(6, 20)$
$= 6 \times 20$. In fact, we can verify that **for any two positive integers $a$ and $b$,**
**HCF $(a, b) \times \text{LCM } (a, b) = a \times b$.** We can use this result to find the LCM of two
positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3: Find the HCF of 96 and 404 by the prime factorisation method. Hence,
find their LCM.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : The prime factorisation of 96 and 404 gives :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the HCF of these two integers is $2^2 = 4$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{Also, } \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{LCM (96, 404)} = \frac{96 \times 404}{\text{HCF(96, 404)}} = \frac{96 \times 404}{4} = 9696 $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120, using the prime factorisation
method.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : We have :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, $2^1$ and $3^1$ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$2^3$, $3^2$ and $5^1$ are the greatest powers of the prime factors 2, 3 and 5 respectively
involved in the three numbers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Remark :** Notice, $6 \times 72 \times 120 \neq \text{HCF } (6, 72, 120) \times \text{LCM } (6, 72, 120)$. So, the
product of three numbers may not be equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.3 Revisiting Irrational Numbers

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties.
You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together
made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number
line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. In this section, we will
prove that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$ and, in general, $\sqrt{p}$ is irrational, where $p$ is a prime. One of
the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall, a number ‘$s$’ is called \textit{irrational} if it cannot be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$,
where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. Some examples of irrational numbers, with
which you are already familiar, are :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Before we prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose
proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Theorem 1.2 :** *Let $p$ be a prime number. If $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where*
*$a$ is a positive integer.*

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: *Proof : Let the prime factorisation of $a$ be as follows :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, where $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$ are primes, not necessarily distinct.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a^2 = (p_1 p_2 \dots p_n)(p_1 p_2 \dots p_n) = p_1^2 p_2^2 \dots p_n^2.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, we are given that $p$ divides $a^2$. Therefore, from the Fundamental Theorem of
Arithmetic, it follows that $p$ is one of the prime factors of $a^2$. However, using the
uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, we realise that the only
prime factors of $a^2$ are $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$. So $p$ is one of $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, since $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, $p$ divides $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We are now ready to give a proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The proof is based on a technique called ‘proof by contradiction’. (This technique is
discussed in some detail in Appendix A1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Theorem 1.3 : $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Not from the examination point of view.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can find integers $r$ and $s$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{2} = \frac{r}{s}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Suppose $r$ and $s$ have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
factor to get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are coprime.
So, $b, \sqrt{2} = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $b \sqrt{2} = a.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get $2b^2 = a^2$. Therefore, 2 divides $a^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by Theorem 1.2, it follows that 2 divides $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can write $a = 2c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $2b^2 = 4c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 2c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This means that 2 divides $b^2$, and so 2 divides $b$ (again using Theorem 1.2 with $p=2$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least 2 as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ have no common factors other than 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Example 5 : Prove that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, we can find integers $a$ and $b$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose $a$ and $b$ have a common factor other than $1$, then we can divide by the
common factor, and assume that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $b\sqrt{3} = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Squaring on both sides, and rearranging, we get $3b^2 = a^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, $a^2$ is divisible by 3, and by Theorem 1.2, it follows that $a$ is also divisible
by 3.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can write $a = 3c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $3b^2 = 9c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 3c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This means that $b^2$ is divisible by 3, and so $b$ is also divisible by 3 (using Theorem 1.2
with $p = 3$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least 3 as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.
So, we conclude that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In Class IX, we mentioned that :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational and

$\bullet$ the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is
irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We prove some particular cases here.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : Show that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is rational.

That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ ($b \neq 0$) such that $5 - \sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

Therefore, $5 - \frac{a}{b} = \sqrt{3}$.

Rearranging this equation, we get $\sqrt{3} = 5 - \frac{a}{b} = \frac{5b - a}{b}$.

Since $a$ and $b$ are integers, we get $5 - \frac{a}{b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is
rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : Show that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $3\sqrt{2}$ is rational.
That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ ($b \neq 0$) such that $3\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$.
Rearranging, we get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{3b}$.
Since $3$, $a$ and $b$ are integers, $\frac{a}{3b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.text: EXERCISE 1.2

2. Prove that $3 + 2\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

3. Prove that the following are irrationals :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

   Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this
factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

2. If $p$ is a prime and $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where $a$ is a positive integer.

3. To prove that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ are irrationals.

You have seen that :

$$HCF (p, q, r) \times \text{LCM} (p, q, r) \neq p \times q \times r, \text{ where } p, q, r \text{ are positive integers}$$
(see Example 4). However, the following results hold good for three numbers

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS 2

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have studied polynomials in one variable and their degrees. Recall
that if $p(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$, the highest power of $x$ in $p(x)$ is called **the degree of**
**the polynomial** $p(x)$. For example, $4x + 2$ is a polynomial in the variable $x$ of
degree $1$, $2y^2 - 3y + 4$ is a polynomial in the variable $y$ of degree $2$, $5x^3 - 4x^2 + x - \sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: is a polynomial in the variable $x$ of degree 3 and $7u^6 - \frac{3}{2}u^4 + 4u^2 + u - 8$ is a polynomial

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
in the variable $u$ of degree 6. Expressions like $\frac{1}{x-1}$, $\sqrt{x}+2$, $\frac{1}{x^2+2x+3}$ etc., are
not polynomials.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A polynomial of degree 1 is called a **linear polynomial**. For example, $2x - 3$,
$\sqrt{3}x + 5$, $y + \sqrt{2}$, $x - \frac{2}{11}, 3z + 4$, $\frac{2}{3}u + 1$, etc., are all linear polynomials. Polynomials
such as $2x + 5 - x^2$, $x^3 + 1$, etc., are not linear polynomials.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A polynomial of degree 2 is called a \textbf{quadratic polynomial}. The name ‘quadratic’
has been derived from the word ‘quadrate’, which means ‘square’. $2x^2 + 3x - \frac{2}{5}$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$y^2 - 2, \ 2-x^2+\sqrt{3}x, \ \frac{u}{3}-2u^2+5, \sqrt{5}v^2-\frac{2}{3}v, 4z^2+\frac{1}{7}$ are some examples of
quadratic polynomials (whose coefficients are real numbers). More generally, any
quadratic polynomial in $x$ is of the form $ax^2+bx+c$, where $a, b, c$ are real numbers
and $a \neq 0$. A polynomial of degree 3 is called a **cubic polynomial**. Some examples of

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
a cubic polynomial are $2-x^3, x^3, \sqrt{2}x^3, 3-x^2+x^3, 3x^3-2x^2+x-1$. In fact, the most
general form of a cubic polynomial is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where, $a, b, c, d$ are real numbers and $a \neq 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now consider the polynomial $p(x) = x^2 - 3x - 4$. Then, putting $x = 2$ in the
polynomial, we get $p(2) = 2^2 - 3 \times 2 - 4 = -6$. The value ‘$-6$’, obtained by replacing
$x$ by $2$ in $x^2 - 3x - 4$, is the value of $x^2 - 3x - 4$ at $x = 2$. Similarly, $p(0)$ is the value of
$p(x)$ at $x = 0$, which is $-4$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $p(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$, and if $k$ is any real number, then the value obtained by
replacing $x$ by $k$ in $p(x)$, is called **the value of $p(x)$ at $x = k$**, and is denoted by $p(k)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: What is the value of $p(x) = x^2 -3x - 4$ at $x = -1$? We have :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Also, note that $p(4) = 4^2 - (3 \times 4) - 4 = 0.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As $p(-1) = 0$ and $p(4) = 0, -1$ and $4$ are called the zeroes of the quadratic
polynomial $x^2 - 3x - 4$. More generally, a real number $k$ is said to be a **zero of a**
**polynomial** $p(x)$, if $p(k) = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already studied in Class IX, how to find the zeroes of a linear
polynomial. For example, if $k$ is a zero of $p(x) = 2x + 3$, then $p(k) = 0$ gives us
$2k + 3 = 0$, i.e., $k = -\frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In general, if $k$ is a zero of $p(x) = ax + b$, then $p(k) = ak + b = 0$, i.e., $k = \frac{-b}{a}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the zero of the linear polynomial $ax + b$ is $\frac{-b}{a} = \frac{-\text{(Constant term)}}{\text{Coefficient of } x}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the zero of a linear polynomial is related to its coefficients. Does this
happen in the case of other polynomials too? For example, are the zeroes of a quadratic
polynomial also related to its coefficients?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, we will try to answer these questions.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.2 Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You know that a real number $k$ is a zero of the polynomial $p(x)$ if $p(k) = 0$. But why
are the zeroes of a polynomial so important? To answer this, first we will see the
**geometrical** representations of linear and quadratic polynomials and the geometrical
meaning of their zeroes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider first a linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$. For example, the graph of $y = 2x + 3$
is a straight line passing through the points $(-2, -1)$ and $(2, 7)$.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Fig. 2.1, you can see

intersects the $x$-axis mid-way

that is, at the point $\left(-\frac{3}{2}, 0\right)$.
You also know that the zero of
$2x + 3$ is $-\frac{3}{2}$. Thus, the zero of
the polynomial $2x + 3$ is the

In general, for a linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$, the graph of $y = ax + b$ is a
straight line which intersects the $x$-axis at exactly one point, namely, $\left(\frac{-b}{a}, 0\right)$.
Therefore, the linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$, has exactly one zero, namely $\frac{-b}{a}$, the
$x$-coordinate of the point where the graph of $y = ax + b$ intersects the $x$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us look for the geometrical meaning of a zero of a quadratic polynomial.
Consider the quadratic polynomial $x^2 - 3x - 4$. Let us see what the graph* of
$y = x^2 - 3x - 4$ looks like. Let us list a few values of $y = x^2 - 3x - 4$ corresponding to

In fact, for any quadratic
polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$, $a \neq 0$, the
graph of the corresponding

of the two shapes either open

This fact is true for any quadratic polynomial, i.e., the zeroes of a quadratic

parabola representing $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ intersects the $x$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observation earlier about the shape of the graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, the
following three cases can happen:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Case (i) : Here, the graph cuts $x$-axis at two distinct points A and A'.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The $x$-coordinates of A and A$'$ are the **two zeroes** of the quadratic polynomial
$ax^2 + bx + c$ in this case (see Fig. 2.3).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case (ii) : Here, the graph cuts the $x$-axis at exactly one point, i.e., at two coincident
points. So, the two points A and A' of Case (i) coincide here to become one point A
(see Fig. 2.4).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The $x$-coordinate of A is the **only zero** for the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$
in this case.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case (iii) : Here, the graph is either completely above the $x$-axis or completely below
the $x$-axis. So, it does not cut the $x$-axis at any point (see Fig. 2.5).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$ has **no zero** in this case.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, you can see geometrically that a quadratic polynomial can have either two
distinct zeroes or two equal zeroes (i.e., one zero), or no zero. This also means that a
polynomial of degree 2 has atmost two zeroes.

blocks.text:

From the examples above, we see that there are at most 3 zeroes for any cubic

intersects the $x$-axis at atmost $n$ points. Therefore, a polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $n$ has
at most $n$ zeroes.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.3 Relationship between Zeroes and Coefficients of a Polynomial

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already seen that zero of a linear polynomial $ax + b$ is $-\frac{b}{a}$. We will now try
to answer the question raised in Section 2.1 regarding the relationship between zeroes
and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial. For this, let us take a quadratic polynomial,
say $p(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 6$. In Class IX, you have learnt how to factorise quadratic
polynomials by splitting the middle term. So, here we need to split the middle term
‘$- 8x$’ as a sum of two terms, whose product is $6 \times 2x^2 = 12x^2$. So, we write

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the value of $p(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 6$ is zero when $x - 1 = 0$ or $x - 3 = 0$, i.e., when
$x = 1$ or $x = 3$. So, the zeroes of $2x^2 - 8x + 6$ are $1$ and $3$. Observe that :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{Sum of its zeroes} \quad = 1 + 3 = 4 = \frac{-(-8)}{2} = \frac{-(\text{Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Product of its zeroes $= 1 \times 3 = 3 = \frac{6}{2} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take one more quadratic polynomial, say, $p(x) = 3x^2 + 5x - 2$. By the
method of splitting the middle term,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the value of $3x^2 + 5x - 2$ is zero when either $3x - 1 = 0$ or $x + 2 = 0$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: when $x = \frac{1}{3}$ or $x = -2$. So, the zeroes of $3x^2 + 5x - 2$ are $\frac{1}{3}$ and $-2$. Observe that :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Sum of its zeroes} \quad = \frac{1}{3} + (-2) = \frac{-5}{3} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Product of its zeroes $= \frac{1}{3} \times (-2) = \frac{-2}{3} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, if $\alpha^*$ and $\beta^*$ are the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$,
$a \neq 0$, then you know that $x - \alpha$ and $x - \beta$ are the factors of $p(x)$. Therefore,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ax^2 + bx + c = k(x - \alpha) (x - \beta), \text{ where } k \text{ is a constant}$$
$$= k[x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha \beta]$$
$$= kx^2 - k(\alpha + \beta)x + k \alpha \beta$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$, $x$ and constant terms on both the sides, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$a = k, b = -k(\alpha + \beta) \text{ and } c = k\alpha\beta.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\alpha + \beta = \frac{-b}{a}$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a} $$

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text:
* $\alpha,\beta$ are Greek letters pronounced as ‘alpha’ and ‘beta’ respectively. We will use later one
more letter ‘$\gamma$’ pronounced as ‘gamma’.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\qquad \qquad \text{sum of zeroes} = \alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a} = \frac{-(\text{Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2},$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: product of zeroes $= \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Find the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $x^2 + 7x + 10$, and verify the
relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.
Solution : We have
$$x^2 + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5)$$
So, the value of $x^2 + 7x + 10$ is zero when $x + 2 = 0$ or $x + 5 = 0$, i.e., when $x = -2$ or
$x = -5$. Therefore, the zeroes of $x^2 + 7x + 10$ are $-2$ and $-5$. Now,

$$\text{sum of zeroes} = -2 + (-5) = -(7) = \frac{-(7)}{1} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2},$$

$$\text{product of zeroes} = (-2) \times (-5) = 10 = \frac{10}{1} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}.$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Find the zeroes of the polynomial $x^2 - 3$ and verify the relationship
between the zeroes and the coefficients.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Recall the identity $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$. Using it, we can write:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the value of $x^2 - 3$ is zero when $x = \sqrt{3}$ or $x = -\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the zeroes of $x^2 - 3$ are $\sqrt{3}$ and $-\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{sum of zeroes} = \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} = 0 = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}, $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: product of zeroes = $(\sqrt{3})(-\sqrt{3}) = -3 = \frac{-3}{1} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : Find a quadratic polynomial, the sum and product of whose zeroes are
$-3$ and $2$, respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let the quadratic polynomial be $ax^2 + bx + c$, and its zeroes be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \alpha + \beta = -3 = \frac{-b}{a}, $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\alpha\beta = 2 = \frac{c}{a}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If $a=1$, then $b=3$ and $c=2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, one quadratic polynomial which fits the given conditions is $x^2 + 3x + 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that any other quadratic polynomial that fits these conditions will
be of the form $k(x^2 + 3x + 2)$, where $k$ is non zero real number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now look at cubic polynomials. Do you think a similar relation holds
between the zeroes of a cubic polynomial and its coefficients?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider $p(x) = 2x^3 - 5x^2 - 14x + 8$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that $p(x) = 0$ for $x = 4, -2, \frac{1}{2}$. Since $p(x)$ can have atmost three

zeroes, these are the zeroes of $2x^3 - 5x^2 - 14x + 8$. Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: sum of the zeroes $= 4 + (-2) + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2} = \frac{-(-5)}{2} = \frac{-(\text{Coefficient of } x^2)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: product of the zeroes $= 4 \times (-2) \times \frac{1}{2} = -4 = \frac{-8}{2} = \frac{-\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
However, there is one more relationship here. Consider the sum of the products
of the zeroes taken two at a time. We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \{4 \times (-2)\} + \left\{ (-2) \times \frac{1}{2} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \right\} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= -8 - 1 + 2 = -7 = \frac{-14}{2} = \frac{\text{Coefficient of } x}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}.$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, it can be proved that if $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial
$ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = \frac{-b}{a}, $$

$$ \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}, $$

$$ \alpha \beta \gamma = \frac{-d}{a}. $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5* : Verify that $3, -1, -\frac{1}{3}$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial
$p(x) = 3x^3 - 5x^2 - 11x - 3$, and then verify the relationship between the zeroes and the
coefficients.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Comparing the given polynomial with $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $3$, $-1$ and $-\frac{1}{3}$ are the zeroes of $3x^3 - 5x^2 - 11x - 3$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, we take $\alpha = 3$, $\beta = -1$ and $\gamma = -\frac{1}{3}$.
Now

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 3 + (-1) + \left( -\frac{1}{3} \right) = 2 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{3} = \frac{-(-5)}{3} = \frac{-b}{a},$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = 3 \times (-1) + (-1) \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) + \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) \times 3 = -3 + \frac{1}{3} - 1 = \frac{-11}{3} = \frac{c}{a},$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha\beta\gamma = 3 \times (-1) \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = 1 = \frac{-(-3)}{3} = \frac{-d}{a}.$$

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Not from the examination point of view.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.4 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Polynomials of degrees 1, 2 and 3 are called linear, quadratic and cubic polynomials
respectively.
2. A quadratic polynomial in $x$ with real coefficients is of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a, b, c$
are real numbers with $a \neq 0$.
3. The zeroes of a polynomial $p(x)$ are precisely the $x$-coordinates of the points, where the
graph of $y = p(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
4. A quadratic polynomial can have at most 2 zeroes and a cubic polynomial can have
at most 3 zeroes.
5. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$, then

$$\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}, \quad \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}.$$

6. If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, then

$$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \frac{-b}{a},$$

$$\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a},$$

and $\quad \alpha\beta\gamma = \frac{-d}{a}.$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.2 Graphical Method of Solution of a Pair of Linear Equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A pair of linear equations which has no solution, is called an $inconsistent$ pair of linear
equations. A pair of linear equations in two variables, which has a solution, is called a
$consistent$ pair of linear equations. A pair of linear equations which are equivalent has
infinitely many distinct common solutions. Such a pair is called a $dependent$ pair of
linear equations in two variables. Note that a dependent pair of linear equations is
always consistent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can now summarise the behaviour of lines representing a pair of linear equations
in two variables and the existence of solutions as follows:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) the lines may intersect in a single point. In this case, the pair of equations
has a unique solution (consistent pair of equations).

(ii) the lines may be parallel. In this case, the equations have no solution
(inconsistent pair of equations).

(iii) the lines may be coincident. In this case, the equations have infinitely many
solutions [dependent (consistent) pair of equations].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the following three pairs of equations.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) $x - 2y = 0$ and $3x + 4y - 20 = 0$ (The lines intersect)
(ii) $2x + 3y - 9 = 0$ and $4x + 6y - 18 = 0$ (The lines coincide)
(iii) $x + 2y - 4 = 0$ and $2x + 4y - 12 = 0$ (The lines are parallel)

blocks.text:

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.3 Algebraic Methods of Solving a Pair of Linear Equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, we discussed how to solve a pair of linear equations graphically.
The graphical method is not convenient in cases when the point representing the
solution of the linear equations has non-integral coordinates like $\left(\sqrt{3}, 2\sqrt{7}\right)$,
$(-1.75, 3.3), \left(\frac{4}{13}, \frac{1}{19}\right)$, etc. There is every possibility of making mistakes while reading

value of the other variable.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.4 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. A pair of linear equations in two variables can be represented, and solved, by the:
(i) graphical method
(ii) algebraic method
2. Graphical Method :
The graph of a pair of linear equations in two variables is represented by two lines.
(i) If the lines intersect at a point, then that point gives the unique solution of the two
equations. In this case, the pair of equations is **consistent**.
(ii) If the lines coincide, then there are infinitely many solutions — each point on
the line being a solution. In this case, the pair of equations is **dependent**
**(consistent)**.
(iii) If the lines are parallel, then the pair of equations has no solution. In this case, the
pair of equations is **inconsistent**.
3. Algebraic Methods : We have discussed the following methods for finding the solution(s)
of a pair of linear equations :
(i) Substitution Method
(ii) Elimination Method
4. If a pair of linear equations is given by $a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0$, then the
following situations can arise :
(i) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \frac{b_1}{b_1}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is consistent.
(ii) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \frac{c_1}{c_2}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is inconsistent.
(iii) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is dependent and consistent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Chapter 2, you have studied different types of polynomials. One type was the
quadratic polynomial of the form $ax^2 + bx + c, a \neq 0$. When we equate this polynomial
to zero, we get a quadratic equation. Quadratic equations come up when we deal with
many real-life situations. For instance, suppose a
charity trust decides to build a prayer hall having
a carpet area of 300 square metres with its length
one metre more than twice its breadth. What
should be the length and breadth of the hall?
Suppose the breadth of the hall is $x$ metres. Then,
its length should be $(2x + 1)$ metres. We can depict
this information pictorially as shown in Fig. 4.1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Many people believe that Babylonians were the first to solve quadratic equations.
For instance, they knew how to find two positive numbers with a given positive sum
and a given positive product, and this problem is equivalent to solving a quadratic
equation of the form $x^2 - px + q = 0$. Greek mathematician Euclid developed a
geometrical approach for finding out lengths which, in our present day terminology,
are solutions of quadratic equations. Solving of quadratic equations, in general form, is
often credited to ancient Indian mathematicians. In fact, Brahmagupta (C.E.598–665)
gave an explicit formula to solve a quadratic equation of the form $ax^2 + bx = c$. Later,

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: QUADRATIC EQUATIONS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Sridharacharya (C.E. 1025) derived a formula, now known as the quadratic formula,
(as quoted by Bhaskara II) for solving a quadratic equation by the method of completing
the square. An  Arab mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (about C.E. 800) also studied
quadratic equations of different types. Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi, in his book
‘Liber embadorum’ published in Europe in C.E. 1145 gave complete solutions of
different quadratic equations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, you will study quadratic equations, and various ways of finding
their roots. You will also see some applications of quadratic equations in daily life
situations.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 4.2 Quadratic Equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ is an equation of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where
$a, b, c$ are real numbers, $a \neq 0$. For example, $2x^2 + x - 300 = 0$ is a quadratic equation.
Similarly, $2x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0$, $4x - 3x^2 + 2 = 0$ and $1 - x^2 + 300 = 0$ are also quadratic
equations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In fact, any equation of the form $p(x) = 0$, where $p(x)$ is a polynomial of degree
2, is a quadratic equation. But when we write the terms of $p(x)$ in descending order of
their degrees, then we get the standard form of the equation. That is, $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$,
$a \neq 0$ is called the **standard form of a quadratic equation.**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Quadratic equations arise in several situations in the world around us and in
different fields of mathematics. Let us consider a few examples.

The number of marbles left with Jivanti, when she lost 5 marbles $= 45 - x - 5$
$= 40 - x$

Therefore, their product $= (x - 5) (40 - x)$
$= 40x - x^2 - 200 + 5x$
$= - x^2 + 45x - 200$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 4.3 Solution of a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider the quadratic equation $2x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0$. If we replace $x$ by $1$ on the
LHS of this equation, we get $(2 \times 1^2) - (3 \times 1) + 1 = 0 =$ RHS of the equation.
We say that $1$ is a root of the quadratic equation $2x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0$. This also means that
$1$ is a zero of the quadratic polynomial $2x^2 - 3x + 1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, a real number $\alpha$ is called a root of the quadratic equation
$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, $a \neq 0$ if $a \alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$. We also say that $x = \alpha$ is a solution of
the quadratic equation, or that $\alpha$ satisfies the quadratic equation. Note that the
zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$ and the roots of the quadratic
equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have observed, in Chapter 2, that a quadratic polynomial can have at most
two zeroes. So, any quadratic equation can have atmost two roots.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have learnt in Class IX, how to factorise quadratic polynomials by splitting
their middle terms. We shall use this knowledge for finding the roots of a quadratic
equation. Let us see how.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Find the roots of the equation $2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$, by factorisation.

Solution : Let us first split the middle term $-5x$ as $-2x$ and $-3x$

$$[\text{because } (-2x) \times (-3x) = 6x^2 = (2x^2) \times 3].$$

So, $2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 2x^2 - 2x - 3x + 3 = 2x(x - 1) - 3(x - 1) = (2x - 3)(x - 1)$

Now, $2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$ can be rewritten as $(2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0$.

So, the values of $x$ for which $2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$ are the same for which $(2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0$,

i.e., either $2x - 3 = 0$ or $x - 1 = 0$.

Now, $2x - 3 = 0$ gives $x = \frac{3}{2}$ and $x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = 1$.

So, $x = \frac{3}{2}$ and $x = 1$ are the solutions of the equation.

In other words, $1$ and $\frac{3}{2}$ are the roots of the equation $2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$.

Verify that these are the roots of the given equation.

$2x^2 - 5x + 3$ into two linear factors and equating each factor to zero.

Therefore, $3x - 2 = 0$ or $2x + 1 = 0$,

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 : Find the roots of the quadratic equation $3x^2 - 2\sqrt{6}x + 2 = 0$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : $3x^2 - 2\sqrt{6}x + 2 = 3x^2 - \sqrt{6}x - \sqrt{6}x + 2$
$= \sqrt{3}x(\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2}) - \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2})$
$= (\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2})(\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2})$

So, the roots of the equation are the values of $x$ for which
$$(\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2})(\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2}) = 0$$

Now, $\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2} = 0$ for $x = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$.

So, this root is repeated twice, one for each repeated factor $\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{2}$.

Therefore, the roots of $3x^2 - 2\sqrt{6}x + 2 = 0$ are $\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$.

blocks.text:
Example 6 : Find the dimensions of the prayer hall discussed in Section 4.1.

Solution : In Section 4.1, we found that if the breadth of the hall is $x$ m, then $x$
satisfies the equation $2x^2 + x - 300 = 0$. Applying the factorisation method, we write
this equation as

$$2x^2 - 24x + 25x - 300 = 0$$
$$2x (x - 12) + 25 (x - 12) = 0$$
i.e.,
$$(x - 12)(2x + 25) = 0$$

So, the roots of the given equation are $x = 12$ or $x = - 12.5$. Since $x$ is the breadth
of the hall, it cannot be negative.

Thus, the breadth of the hall is $12$ m. Its length $= 2x + 1 = 25$ m.

blocks.text: Thus, the breadth of the hall is 12 m. Its length $= 2x + 1 = 25$ m.

blocks.text: 4.4 Nature of Roots

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: If $b^2 - 4ac > 0$, we get two distinct real roots $-\frac{b}{2a} + \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$ and

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ -\frac{b}{2a} - \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}. $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: If $b^2 - 4ac = 0$, then $x = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm 0$, i.e., $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$ or $-\frac{b}{2a}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are both $\frac{-b}{2a}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, we say that the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has two equal
real roots in this case.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, then there is no real number whose square is $b^2 - 4ac$. Therefore,
there are no real roots for the given quadratic equation in this case.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since $b^2 - 4ac$ determines whether the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has
real roots or not, $b^2 - 4ac$ is called the **discriminant** of this quadratic equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) two distinct real roots, if $b^2 - 4ac > 0$,
(ii) two equal real roots, if $b^2 - 4ac = 0$,
(iii) no real roots, if $b^2 - 4ac < 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

$c = 3$. Therefore, the discriminant
$$b^2 - 4ac = (- 4)^2 - (4 \times 2 \times 3) = 16 - 24 = - 8 < 0$$
So, the given equation has no real roots.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 4.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ is of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a, b, c$ are real numbers and $a \neq 0$.

2. A real number $\alpha$ is said to be a root of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, if $\alpha\alpha^2 + b\alpha + c = 0$. The zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$ and the roots of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are the same.

3. If we can factorise $ax^2 + bx + c$, $a \neq 0$, into a product of two linear factors, then the roots of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ can be found by equating each factor to zero.

4. Quadratic formula: The roots of a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are given by $\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$, provided $b^2 - 4ac \geq 0$.

5. A quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has
   (i) two distinct real roots, if $b^2 - 4ac > 0$,
   (ii) two equal roots (i.e., coincident roots), if $b^2 - 4ac = 0$, and
   (iii) no real roots, if $b^2 - 4ac < 0$.

In the examples above, we observe some patterns. In some, we find that the

blocks.label: Paragraph

In this chapter, we shall discuss one of these patterns in which succeeding terms

to find their $n$th terms and the sum of $n$ consecutive terms, and use this knowledge in
solving some daily life problems.

blocks.label: Section-title

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the following lists of numbers :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Each of the numbers in the list is called a **term**.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Given a term, can you write the next term in each of the lists above? If so, how
will you write it? Perhaps by following a pattern or rule. Let us observe and write the
rule.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In (i), each term is 1 more than the term preceding it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In (ii), each term is 30 less than the term preceding it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In (iii), each term is obtained by adding 1 to the term preceding it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In (iv), all the terms in the list are 3 , i.e., each term is obtained by adding
(or subtracting) 0 to the term preceding it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In (v), each term is obtained by adding $- 0.5$ to (i.e., subtracting $0.5$ from) the
term preceding it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In all the lists above, we see that successive terms are obtained by adding a fixed
number to the preceding terms. Such list of numbers is said to form an **Arithmetic**
**Progression ( AP )**.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term  is
obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first
term.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This fixed number is called the **common difference** of the AP. Remember that
it **can be positive, negative or zero**.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us denote the first term of an AP by $a_1$, second term by $a_2, \dots, n$th term by
$a_n$ and the common difference by $d$. Then the AP becomes $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Some more examples of AP are:

blocks.text:

$$ - 3.1, - 3.0, - 2.9, - 2.8, - 2.7, - 2.6, - 2.5 $$

month is 950, 900, 850, 800, . . . , 50.

respectively 200, 250, 300, 350, . . . , 750.

(e) The total savings (in ₹) after every month for 10 months when ₹ 50 are saved
each month are 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500.

blocks.text: 5.3 $n$th Term of an AP

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us consider the situation again, given in Section 5.1 in which Reena applied for a
job and got selected. She has been offered the job with a starting monthly salary of
₹ 8000, with an annual increment of ₹ 500. What would be her monthly salary for the
fifth year?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To answer this, let us first see what her monthly salary for the second year
would be.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
It would be ₹ $(8000 + 500) = \text{₹ } 8500$. In the same way, we can find the monthly
salary for the 3rd, 4th and 5th year by adding ₹ 500 to the salary of the previous year.
So, the salary for the 3rd year = ₹ $(8500 + 500)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Salary for the 4th year $= \text{₹ } (9000 + 500)$
$= \text{₹ } (8000 + 500 + 500 + 500)$
$= \text{₹ } (8000 + 3 \times 500)$
$= \text{₹ } [8000 + (4 - 1) \times 500] \quad \text{(for the \textbf{4th year})} $
$= \text{₹ } 9500$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Observe that we are getting a list of numbers

This example would have given you some idea about how to write the 15th term,
or the 25th term, and more generally, the $n$th term of the AP.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an AP whose first term $a_1$ is $a$ and the common
difference is $d$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
the second term $a_{2}=a+d=a+(\mathbf{2}-\mathbf{1}) d$
the third term $a_{3}=a_{2}+d=(a+d)+d=a+2 d=a+(\mathbf{3}-\mathbf{1}) d$
the fourth term $a_{4}=a_{3}+d=(a+2 d)+d=a+3 d=a+(\mathbf{4}-\mathbf{1}) d$
$\ldots$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Looking at the pattern, we can say that the $\boldsymbol{n}$th term $a_n = a + (n - 1) d$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the $n$th term $a_n$ of the AP with first term $a$ and common difference $d$ is
given by $a_n = a + (n - 1) d$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\boldsymbol{a}_n$ is also called the **general term of the AP**. If there are $m$ terms in the AP, then
$\boldsymbol{a}_m$ represents the **last term which is sometimes also denoted by** $l$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

We have $\quad a_n = a + (n - 1) d$

So, $\quad a_{10} = 2 + (10 - 1) \times 5 = 2 + 45 = 47$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the 10th term of the given AP is 47.

Solution : The list of two-digit numbers divisible by 3 is :
$$12, 15, 18, \dots, 99$$
Is this an AP? Yes it is. Here, $a = 12, d = 3, a_n = 99.$
As $a_n = a + (n - 1) d,$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.4 Sum of First $n$ Terms of an AP

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us consider the situation again
given in Section 5.1 in which Shakila
put ₹ 100 into her daughter's money
box when she was one year old,
₹ 150 on her second birthday,
₹ 200 on her third birthday and will
continue in the same way. How much
money will be collected in the money
box by the time her daughter is 21
years old?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, the amount of money (in ₹) put in the money box on her first, second, third,
fourth . . . birthday were respectively 100, 150, 200, 250, . . . till her 21st birthday. To
find the total amount in the money box on her 21st birthday, we will have to write each
of the 21 numbers in the list above and then add them up. Don’t you think it would be
a tedious and time consuming process? Can we make the process shorter? This would
be possible if we can find a method for getting this sum. Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We consider the problem given to Gauss (about whom you read in
Chapter 1), to solve when he was just 10 years old. He was asked to find the sum of
the positive integers from 1 to 100. He immediately replied that the sum is 5050. Can
you guess how did he do? He wrote :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: And then, reversed the numbers to write

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Adding these two, he got

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We will now use the same technique to find the sum of the first $n$ terms of an AP :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$a, a + d, a + 2d, \dots$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The $n$th term of this AP is $a + (n - 1) d$. Let S denote the sum of the first $n$ terms
of the AP. We have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Rewriting the terms in reverse order, we have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: On adding (1) and (2), term-wise. we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2\mathrm{S} = \underbrace{[2a + (n - 1)d] + [2a + (n - 1)d] + ... + [2a + (n - 1)d] + [2a + (n - 1)d]}_{n \text{ times}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $2\mathrm{S} = n [2a + (n - 1) d]$ (Since, there are $n$ equal terms)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the sum of the first $n$ terms of an AP is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{S} = \frac{n}{2} [2a + (n-1) d] $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
We can also write this as
$$S = \frac{n}{2} [a + a + (n - 1) d]$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
i.e.,
$$S = \frac{n}{2} (a + a_n) \eqno(3)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if there are only $n$ terms in an AP, then $a_n = l$, the last term.
From (3), we see that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{S} = \frac{\mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{2}} (a + l) \tag{4} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This form of the result is useful when the first and the last terms of an AP are
given and the common difference is not given.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now we return to the question that was posed to us in the beginning. The amount
of money (in Rs) in the money box of Shakila’s daughter on 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th birthday,
. . ., were 100, 150, 200, 250, . . ., respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This is an AP. We have to find the total money collected on her 21st birthday, i.e.,
the sum of the first 21 terms of this AP.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: ARITHMETIC PROGRESSIONS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, $a=100$, $d=50$ and $n=21$. Using the formula :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: we have $\qquad \mathrm{S} = \frac{21}{2} [2 \times 100 + (21 - 1) \times 50] = \frac{21}{2} [200 + 1000]$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the amount of money collected on her 21st birthday is ₹ 12600.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hasn't the use of the formula made it much easier to solve the problem?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We also use $\mathrm{S}_n$ in place of $\mathrm{S}$ to denote the sum of first $n$ terms of the AP. We
write $\mathrm{S}_{20}$ to denote the sum of the first 20 terms of an AP. The formula for the sum of
the first $n$ terms involves four quantities $\mathrm{S}$, $a$, $d$ and $n$. If we know any three of them,
we can find the fourth.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : The $n$th term of an AP is the difference of the sum to first $n$ terms and the
sum to first $(n-1)$ terms of it, i.e., $a_n = \mathrm{S}_n - \mathrm{S}_{n-1}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 11 : Find the sum of the first 22 terms of the AP : $8, 3, -2, \dots$
Solution : Here, $a = 8$, $d = 3 - 8 = -5$, $n = 22$.

We know that

$$S = \frac{n}{2} [2a + (n - 1) d]$$

Therefore, $S = \frac{22}{2} [16 + 21 (-5)] = 11(16 - 105) = 11(-89) = -979$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the sum of the first 22 terms of the AP is – 979.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 : If the sum of the first 14 terms of an AP is 1050 and its first term is 10,
find the 20th term.

Solution : Here, $S_{14} = 1050$, $n = 14$, $a = 10$.

As $S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$,

so, $1050 = \frac{14}{2}[20 + 13d] = 140 + 91d$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $a_{20} = 10 + (20 - 1) \times 10 = 200$, i.e. 20th term is 200.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

sum is 78?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Solution :** Here, $a = 24$, $d = 21 - 24 = -3$, $S_n = 78$. We need to find $n$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We know that $S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Both values of $n$ are admissible. So, the number of terms is either 4 or 13.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. In this case, the sum of the first 4 terms $=$ the sum of the first 13 terms $=$ 78.
2. Two answers are possible because the sum of the terms from 5th to 13th will be
zero. This is because $a$ is positive and $d$ is negative, so that some terms will be
positive and some others negative, and will cancel out each other.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the sum of first $n$ positive integers is given by

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 5.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by
adding a fixed number $d$ to the preceding term, except the first term. The fixed number $d$
is called the common difference.

The general form of an AP is $a$, $a+d$, $a+2d$, $a+3d$, $\dots$

2. A given list of numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dots$ is an AP, if the differences $a_2 - a_1$, $a_3 - a_2$,
$a_4 - a_3$, $\dots$ give the same value, i.e., if $a_{k+1} - a_k$ is the same for different values of $k$.

3. In an AP with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, the $n$th term (or the general term) is
given by $a_n = a + (n-1)d$.

4. The sum of the first $n$ terms of an AP is given by :

$$S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$$

5. If $l$ is the last term of the finite AP, say the $n$th term, then the sum of all terms of the AP
is given by :

$$S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)$$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
A NOTE TO THE READER

If $a, b, c$ are in AP, then $b = \frac{a + c}{2}$ and $b$ is called the arithmetic
mean of $a$ and $c$.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: TRIANGLES 6

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 6.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You are familiar with triangles and many of their properties from your earlier classes.
In Class IX, you have studied congruence of triangles in detail. Recall that two figures
are said to be \textit{congruent}, if they have the same shape and the same size. In this
chapter, we shall study about those figures which have the same shape but not
necessarily the same size. Two figures having the same shape (and not necessarily
the same size) are called \textit{similar figures}. In particular, we shall discuss the similarity
of triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Can you guess how heights of mountains (say Mount Everest) or distances of
some long distant objects (say moon) have been found out? Do you think these have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
been measured directly with the help of a measuring tape? In fact, all these heights
and distances have been found out using the idea of indirect measurements, which is
based on the principle of similarity of figures (see Example 7, Q.15 of Exercise 6.3
and also Chapters 8 and 9 of this book).

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 6.2 Similar Figures

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have seen that all circles with the same radii are congruent, all
squares with the same side lengths are congruent and all equilateral triangles with the
same side lengths are congruent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now consider any two (or more)
circles [see Fig. 6.1 (i)]. Are they
congruent? Since all of them do not
have the same radius, they are not
congruent to each other. Note that
some are congruent and some are not,
but all of them have the same shape.
So they all are, what we call, \textit{similar}.
Two similar figures have the same
shape but not necessarily the same
size. Therefore, all circles are similar.
What about two (or more) squares or
two (or more) equilateral triangles
[see Fig. 6.1 (ii) and (iii)]? As observed
in the case of circles, here also all
squares are similar and all equilateral
triangles are similar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the above, we can say
that all congruent figures are
similar but the similar figures need
not be congruent.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Can a circle and a square be
similar? Can a triangle and a square
be similar? These questions can be
answered by just looking at the
figures (see Fig. 6.1). Evidently
these figures are not similar. (Why?)

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.2

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: TRIANGLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What can you say about the two quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS
(see Fig 6.2)?Are they similar? These figures appear to be similar but we cannot be
certain about it.Therefore, we must have some definition of similarity of figures and
based on this definition some rules to decide whether the two given figures are similar
or not. For this, let us look at the photographs given in Fig. 6.3:

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You will at once say that they are the photographs of the same monument
(Taj Mahal) but are in different sizes. Would you say that the three photographs are
similar? Yes,they are.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What can you say about the two photographs of the same size of the same
person one at the age of 10 years and the other at the age of 40 years? Are these
photographs similar? These photographs are of the same size but certainly they are
not of the same shape. So, they are not similar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What does the photographer do when she prints photographs of different sizes
from the same negative? You must have heard about the stamp size, passport size and
postcard size photographs. She generally takes a photograph on a small size film, say
of $35\text{mm}$ size and then enlarges it into a bigger size, say $45\text{mm}$ (or $55\text{mm}$). Thus, if we
consider any line segment in the smaller photograph (figure), its corresponding line

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: The segment in the bigger photograph (figure) will be $\frac{45}{35}\left(\text{or } \frac{55}{35}\right)$ of that of the line segment.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This really means that every line segment of the smaller photograph is enlarged
(increased) \textit{in the ratio} 35:45 (or 35:55). It can also be said that every line segment
of the bigger photograph is reduced (decreased) in the ratio 45:35 (or 55:35). Further,
if you consider inclinations (or angles) between any pair of corresponding line segments
in the two photographs of different sizes, you shall see that these inclinations(or angles)
\textit{are always equal}. This is the essence of the similarity of two figures and in particular
of two polygons. We say that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their
corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the
same ratio (or proportion).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the same ratio of the corresponding sides is referred to as the scale
factor (or the Representative Fraction) for the polygons. You must have heard that
world maps (i.e., global maps) and blue prints for the construction of a building are
prepared using a suitable scale factor and observing certain conventions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In order to understand similarity of figures more clearly, let us perform the following
activity:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 1 : Place a lighted bulb at a
point O on the ceiling and directly below
it a table in your classroom. Let us cut a
polygon, say a quadrilateral ABCD, from
a plane cardboard and place this
cardboard parallel to the ground between
the lighted bulb and the table. Then a
shadow of ABCD is cast on the table.
Mark the outline of this shadow as
$A'B'C'D'$ (see Fig.6.4).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the quadrilateral $A'B'C'D'$ is
an enlargement (or magnification) of the
quadrilateral ABCD. This is because of
the property of light that light propagates
in a straight line. You may also note that
$A'$ lies on ray OA, $B'$ lies on ray OB, $C'$
lies on OC and $D'$ lies on OD. Thus, quadrilaterals $A'B'C'D'$ and ABCD are of the
same shape but of different sizes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, quadrilateral $A'B'C'D'$ is similiar to quadrilateral ABCD. We can also say
that quadrilateral ABCD is similar to the quadrilateral $A'B'C'D'$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, you can also note that vertex $A'$ corresponds to vertex $A$, vertex $B'$
corresponds to vertex $B$, vertex $C'$ corresponds to vertex $C$ and vertex $D'$ corresponds
to vertex $D$. Symbolically, these correspondences are represented as $A' \leftrightarrow A, B' \leftrightarrow B,$
$C' \leftrightarrow C$ and $D' \leftrightarrow D$. By actually measuring the angles and the sides of the two
quadrilaterals, you may verify that

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) $\angle A = \angle A'$, $\angle B = \angle B'$, $\angle C = \angle C'$, $\angle D = \angle D'$ and
(ii) $\frac{AB}{A'B'} = \frac{BC}{B'C'} = \frac{CD}{C'D'} = \frac{DA}{D'A'}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This again emphasises that two polygons of the same number of sides are
similar, if (i) all the corresponding angles are equal and (ii) all the corresponding
sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the above, you can easily say that quadrilaterals ABCD and PQRS of
Fig. 6.5 are similar.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : You can verify that if one polygon is similar to another polygon and this
second polygon is similar to a third polygon, then the first polygon is similar to the third
polygon.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may note that in the two quadrilaterals (a square and a rectangle) of
Fig. 6.6, corresponding angles are equal, but their corresponding sides are not in the
same ratio.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the two quadrilaterals are not similar. Similarly, you may note that in the two
quadrilaterals (a square and a rhombus) of Fig. 6.7, corresponding sides are in the
same ratio, but their corresponding angles are not equal. Again, the two polygons
(quadrilaterals) are not similar.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.7

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, either of the above two conditions (i) and (ii) of similarity of two
polygons is not sufficient for them to be similar.
