blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 6.3 Similarity of Triangles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: What can you say about the similarity of two triangles?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may recall that triangle is also a polygon. So, we can state the same conditions
for the similarity of two triangles. That is:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Two triangles are similiar, if

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$(i)$ their corresponding angles are equal and
$(ii)$ their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that if corresponding angles of two
triangles are equal, then they are known as
equiangular triangles. A famous Greek
mathematician Thales gave an important truth relating
to two equiangular triangles which is as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The ratio of any two corresponding sides in
two equiangular triangles is always the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
It is believed that he had used a result called
the $Basic$ $Proportionality$ $Theorem$ (now known as
the $Thales$ $Theorem$) for the same.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text:
Thales
(B.C.E. 640 – B.C.E. 546)

Theorem, let us perform the following activity:

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 6.4 Criteria for Similarity of Triangles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, we stated that two triangles are similar, if (i) their corresponding
angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, in $\Delta$ ABC and $\Delta$ DEF, if

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
That is, in $\Delta$ ABC and $\Delta$ DEF, if
(i) $\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$, $\angle C = \angle F$ and

(ii) $\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{EF} = \frac{CA}{FD}$, then the two triangles are similar (see Fig. 6.22).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, you can see that A corresponds to D, B corresponds to E and C
corresponds to F. Symbolically, we write the similarity of these two triangles as
‘$\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ DEF’ and read it as ‘triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF’. The
symbol ‘$\sim$’ stands for ‘is similar to’. Recall that you have used the symbol ‘$\equiv$’ for
‘is congruent to’ in Class IX.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
It must be noted that as done in the case of congruency of two triangles, the
similarity of two triangles should also be expressed symbolically, using correct
correspondence of their vertices. For example, for the triangles ABC and DEF of
Fig. 6.22, we cannot write $\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ EDF or $\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ FED. However, we
can write $\Delta$ BAC $\sim$ $\Delta$ EDF.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now a natural question arises : For checking the similarity of two triangles, say
ABC and DEF, should we always look for all the equality relations of their corresponding
angles ($\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$, $\angle C = \angle F$) and all the equality relations of the ratios

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: of their corresponding sides $\left( \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{EF}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}} \right)$? Let us examine. You may recall that

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
in Class IX, you have obtained some criteria for congruency of two triangles involving
only three pairs of corresponding parts (or elements) of the two triangles. Here also,
let us make an attempt to arrive at certain criteria for similarity of two triangles involving
relationship between less number of pairs of corresponding parts of the two triangles,
instead of all the six pairs of corresponding parts. For this, let us perform the following
activity:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 4 : Draw two line segments BC and EF of two different lengths, say 3 cm
and 5 cm respectively. Then, at the points B and C respectively, construct angles PBC
and QCB of some measures, say, $60^\circ$ and $40^\circ$. Also, at the points E and F, construct
angles REF and SFE of $60^\circ$ and $40^\circ$ respectively (see Fig. 6.23).

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: TRIANGLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let rays BP and CQ intersect each other at A and rays ER and FS intersect each
other at D. In the two triangles ABC and DEF, you can see that
$\angle \text{B} = \angle \text{E}$, $\angle \text{C} = \angle \text{F}$ and $\angle \text{A} = \angle \text{D}$. That is, corresponding angles of these two
triangles are equal. What can you say about their corresponding sides ? Note that
$\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{EF}} = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6$. What about $\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}}$ and $\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}}$? On measuring AB, DE, CA and FD, you
will find that $\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}}$ and $\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}}$ are also equal to 0.6 (or nearly equal to 0.6, if there is some
error in the measurement). Thus, $\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{EF}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}}$. You can repeat this activity by
constructing several pairs of triangles having their corresponding angles equal. Every
time, you will find that their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
This activity leads us to the following criterion for similarity of two triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 6.3 :** *If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their*
*corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion) and hence the two*
*triangles are similar.*
**D**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This criterion is referred to as the AAA
(Angle–Angle–Angle) criterion of
similarity of two triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This theorem can be proved by taking two
triangles ABC and DEF such that
$\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$ and $\angle C = \angle F$
(see Fig. 6.24)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Cut DP = AB and DQ = AC and join PQ.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \Delta \text{ABC} \cong \Delta \text{DPQ} \qquad \text{(Why ?)}$
This gives $\qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \angle \text{B} = \angle \text{P} = \angle \text{E} \text{ and } \text{PQ} \parallel \text{EF} \quad \text{(How?)}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{DP}}{\mathrm{PE}} = \frac{\mathrm{DQ}}{\mathrm{QF}}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{DE}} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{DF}}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{DE}}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{EF}}$ and so $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{DE}}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{EF}}=\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{DF}}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : If two angles of a triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another
triangle, then by the angle sum property of a triangle their third angles will also be
equal. Therefore, AAA similarity criterion can also be stated as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another
triangle, then the two triangles are similar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This may be referred to as the AA similarity criterion for two triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have seen above that if the three angles of one triangle are respectively
equal to the three angles of another triangle, then their corresponding sides are
proportional (i.e., in the same ratio). What about the converse of this statement? Is the
converse true? In other words, if the sides of a triangle are respectively proportional to
the sides of another triangle, is it true that their corresponding angles are equal? Let us
examine it through an activity :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 5 : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm,
CA = 8 cm, DE = 4.5 cm, EF = 9 cm and FD = 12 cm (see Fig. 6.25).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, you have : $\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{EF}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}}$ (each equal to $\frac{2}{3}$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now measure $\angle$ A, $\angle$ B, $\angle$ C, $\angle$ D, $\angle$ E and $\angle$ F. You will observe that
$\angle$ A = $\angle$ D, $\angle$ B = $\angle$ E and $\angle$ C = $\angle$ F, i.e., the corresponding angles of the two
triangles are equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can repeat this activity by drawing several such triangles (having their sides
in the same ratio). Everytime you shall see that their corresponding angles are equal.
It is due to the following criterion of similarity of two triangles:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 6.4 :** *If in two triangles, sides of one triangle are proportional to*
*(i.e., in the same ratio of) the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding*
*angles are equal and hence the two triangles are similar.*

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This criterion is referred to as the SSS (Side–Side–Side) similarity criterion for
two triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This theorem can be proved by taking two triangles ABC and DEF such that
$$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{EF}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{FD}} \quad (< 1) \text{ (see Fig. 6.26):}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Cut DP = AB and DQ = AC and join PQ.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: It can be seen that $\frac{\mathrm{DP}}{\mathrm{PE}} = \frac{\mathrm{DQ}}{\mathrm{QF}}$ and $\mathrm{PQ} \parallel \mathrm{EF}$ (How?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle P = \angle E$ and $\angle Q = \angle F.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{DP}}{\mathrm{DE}} = \frac{\mathrm{DQ}}{\mathrm{DF}} = \frac{\mathrm{PQ}}{\mathrm{EF}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{DP}}{\mathrm{DE}} = \frac{\mathrm{DQ}}{\mathrm{DF}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{EF}}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So,                                     $BC = PQ$          (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Thus, $\Delta \text{ABC} \cong \Delta \text{DPQ} \quad (\text{Why } ?)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$ and $\angle C = \angle F$ (How ?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : You may recall that either of the two conditions namely, (i) corresponding
angles are equal and (ii) corresponding sides are in the same ratio is not sufficient for
two polygons to be similar. However, on the basis of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, you can
now say that in case of similarity of the two triangles, it is not necessary to check both
the conditions as one condition implies the other.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now recall the various criteria for congruency of two triangles learnt in
Class IX. You may observe that SSS similarity criterion can be compared with the SSS
congruency criterion.This suggests us to look for a similarity criterion comparable to
SAS congruency criterion of triangles. For this, let us perform an activity.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 6 : Draw two triangles ABC and DEF such that AB = 2 cm, $\angle$ A = $50^\circ$,
AC = 4 cm, DE = 3 cm, $\angle$ D = $50^\circ$ and DF = 6 cm (see Fig.6.27).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, you may observe that $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{DE}} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{DF}}$ (each equal to $\frac{2}{3}$) and $\angle \mathrm{A}$ (included
between the sides $\mathrm{AB}$ and $\mathrm{AC}$) $= \angle \mathrm{D}$ (included between the sides $\mathrm{DE}$ and $\mathrm{DF}$). That
is, one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and sides including
these angles are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion). Now let us measure $\angle \mathrm{B}$, $\angle \mathrm{C}$,
$\angle \mathrm{E}$ and $\angle \mathrm{F}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You will find that $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{E}$ and $\angle \mathrm{C} = \angle \mathrm{F}$. That is, $\angle \mathrm{A} = \angle \mathrm{D}$, $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{E}$ and
$\angle \mathrm{C} = \angle \mathrm{F}$. So, by AAA similarity criterion, $\Delta \mathrm{ABC} \sim \Delta \mathrm{DEF}$. You may repeat this
activity by drawing several pairs of such triangles with one angle of a triangle equal to
one angle of another triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional.
Everytime, you will find that the triangles are similar. It is due to the following criterion
of similarity of triangles:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 6.5 :** *If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of the other*
*triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two*
*triangles are similar.*

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This criterion is referred to as
the SAS (Side-Angle-Side)
similarity criterion for two
triangles.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As before, this theorem can
be proved by taking two triangles
ABC and DEF such that

$$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{DF}} \quad (< 1) \text{ and } \angle \text{A} = \angle \text{D}$$

(see Fig. 6.28). Cut DP = AB, DQ
= AC and join PQ.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\qquad \qquad \qquad \text{PQ } \parallel \text{ EF and } \Delta \text{ ABC } \cong \Delta \text{ DPQ} \qquad \text{(How ?)}$
So, $\qquad \qquad \quad \angle \text{ A } = \angle \text{ D}, \angle \text{ B } = \angle \text{ P and } \angle \text{ C } = \angle \text{ Q}$
Therefore, $\qquad \quad \Delta \text{ ABC } \sim \Delta \text{ DEF} \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{(Why?)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We now take some examples to illustrate the use of these criteria.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 4 : In Fig. 6.29, if PQ $\parallel$ RS, prove that $\Delta$ POQ $\sim \Delta$ SOR.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
**Solution :**                                     PQ $\parallel$ RS                                                                                                                            (Given)
So,                                          $\angle \text{P} = \angle \text{S}$                                                                                                                            (Alternate angles)
and                                          $\angle \text{Q} = \angle \text{R}$
Also,                                     $\angle \text{POQ} = \angle \text{SOR}$                                                                                                                            (Vertically opposite angles)
Therefore,                                  $\Delta \text{POQ} \sim \Delta \text{SOR}$                                                                                                                            (AAA similarity criterion)

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 : Observe Fig. 6.30 and then find $\angle$ P.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : In $\Delta$ ABC and $\Delta$ PQR,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{RQ}} = \frac{3.8}{7.6} = \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QP}} = \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: That is, $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{RQ}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QP}} = \frac{\mathrm{CA}}{\mathrm{PR}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, $\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ RQP (SSS similarity)

Therefore, $\angle$ C = $\angle$ P (Corresponding angles of similar triangles)

But $\angle$ C = $180^{\circ} - \angle$ A – $\angle$ B (Angle sum property)

$= 180^{\circ} - 80^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 40^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : In Fig. 6.31,
$$OA \ . \ OB = OC \ . \ OD.$$
Show that $\angle A = \angle C$ and $\angle B = \angle D.$
Solution : $OA \ . \ OB = OC \ . \ OD$ (Given)

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 6.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar
figures.
2. All the congruent figures are similar but the converse is not true.
3. Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles
are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (i.e., proportion).
4. If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in
distinct points, then the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
5. If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the
third side.
6. If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in
the same ratio and hence the two triangles are similar (AAA similarity criterion).
7. If in two triangles, two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to the two angles of
the other triangle, then the two triangles are similar (AA similarity criterion).

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
8. If in two triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio, then their corresponding
angles are equal and hence the triangles are similar (SSS similarity criterion).
9. If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and the sides including
these angles are in the same ratio (proportional), then the triangles are similar
(SAS similarity criterion).

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
A NOTE TO THE READER

If in two right triangles, hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are
proportional to the hypotenuse and one side of the other triangle,
then the two triangles are similar. This may be referred to as the
RHS Similarity Criterion.

If you use this criterion in Example 2, Chapter 8, the proof will become
simpler.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have studied that, to locate the position of a point on a plane, we
require a pair of coordinate axes. The distance of a point from the $y$-axis is called its
$\boldsymbol{x}$\textbf{-coordinate}, or $\boldsymbol{abscissa}$. The distance of a point from the $x$-axis is called its
$\boldsymbol{y}$\textbf{-coordinate}, or $\boldsymbol{ordinate}$. The coordinates of a point on the $x$-axis are of the form
$(x, 0)$, and of a point on the $y$-axis are of the form $(0, y)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here is a play for you. Draw a set of a pair of perpendicular axes on a graph
paper. Now plot the following points and join them as directed: Join the point $A(4, 8)$ to
$B(3, 9)$ to $C(3, 8)$ to $D(1, 6)$ to $E(1, 5)$ to $F(3, 3)$ to $G(6, 3)$ to $H(8, 5)$ to $I(8, 6)$ to
$J(6, 8)$ to $K(6, 9)$ to $L(5, 8)$ to $A$. Then join the points $P(3.5, 7)$, $Q$ $(3, 6)$ and $R(4, 6)$ to
form a triangle. Also join the points $X(5.5, 7)$, $Y(5, 6)$ and $Z(6, 6)$ to form a triangle.
Now join $S(4, 5)$, $T(4.5, 4)$ and $U(5, 5)$ to form a triangle. Lastly join $S$ to the points
$(0, 5)$ and $(0, 6)$ and join $U$ to the points $(9, 5)$ and $(9, 6)$. What picture have you got?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, you have seen that a linear equation in two variables of the form
$ax + by + c = 0$, ($a, b$ are not simultaneously zero), when represented graphically,
gives a straight line. Further, in Chapter 2, you have seen the graph of
$y = ax^2 + bx + c$ ($a \neq 0$), is a parabola. In fact, coordinate geometry has been developed
as an algebraic tool for studying geometry of figures. It helps us to study geometry
using algebra, and understand algebra with the help of geometry. Because of this,
coordinate geometry is widely applied in various fields such as physics, engineering,
navigation, seismology and art!

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, you will learn how to find the distance between the two points
whose coordinates are given. You will also study how to find the coordinates of the
point which divides a line segment joining two given points in a given ratio.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Do the points $(3, 2), (-2, -3)$ and $(2, 3)$ form a triangle? If so, name the
type of triangle formed.
Solution : Let us apply the distance formula to find the distances PQ, QR and PR,
where P(3, 2), Q$(-2, -3)$ and R(2, 3) are the given points. We have

$$PQ = \sqrt{(3 + 2)^2 + (2 + 3)^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{50} = 7.07 \text{ (approx.)}$$

$$QR = \sqrt{(-2 - 2)^2 + (-3 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-6)^2} = \sqrt{52} = 7.21 \text{ (approx.)}$$

$$PR = \sqrt{(3 - 2)^2 + (2 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2} = 1.41 \text{ (approx.)}$$

Since the sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third distance, therefore,
the points P, Q and R form a triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since the sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third distance, therefore,
the points P, Q and R form a triangle.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, $\mathrm{PQ}^2 + \mathrm{PR}^2 = \mathrm{QR}^2$, by the converse of Pythagoras theorem, we have $\angle \mathrm{P} = 90^\circ$.
Therefore, PQR is a right triangle.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Show that the points $(1, 7), (4, 2), (-1, -1)$ and $(- 4, 4)$ are the vertices
of a square.

Solution : Let $A(1, 7), B(4, 2), C(-1, -1)$ and $D(- 4, 4)$ be the given points. One way
of showing that ABCD is a square is to use the property that all its sides should be
equal and both its diagonals should also be equal. Now,

$$AB = \sqrt{(1 - 4)^2 + (7 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}$$

$$BC = \sqrt{(4 + 1)^2 + (2 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}$$

$$CD = \sqrt{(-1 + 4)^2 + (-1 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}$$

$$DA = \sqrt{(1 + 4)^2 + (7 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}$$

$$AC = \sqrt{(1 + 1)^2 + (7 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 64} = \sqrt{68}$$

$$BD = \sqrt{(4 + 4)^2 + (2 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 4} = \sqrt{68}$$

Since, $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $AC = BD$, all the four sides of the quadrilateral
ABCD are equal and its diagonals AC and BD are also equal. Thereore, ABCD is a
square.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since, $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $AC = BD$, all the four sides of the quadrilateral
ABCD are equal and its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are also equal. Thereore, $ABCD$ is a
square.

34 + 34 = 68 = AC$^2$. Therefore, by
the converse of Pythagoras
theorem, $\angle$ D = 90$^\circ$. A quadrilateral
with all four sides equal and one
angle 90$^\circ$ is a square. So, ABCD
is a square.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : Find a relation between $x$ and $y$ such that the point $(x, y)$ is equidistant
from the points $(7, 1)$ and $(3, 5)$.

Solution : Let $P(x, y)$ be equidistant from the points $A(7, 1)$ and $B(3, 5)$.

We are given that $AP = BP$. So, $AP^2 = BP^2$

i.e., $$(x - 7)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + (y - 5)^2$$

i.e., $$x^2 - 14x + 49 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = x^2 - 6x + 9 + y^2 - 10y + 25$$

i.e., $$x - y = 2$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the required relation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Remark :** Note that the graph of the equation
$x-y=2$ is a line. From your earlier studies,
you know that a point which is equidistant
from A and B lies on the perpendicular
bisector of AB. Therefore, the graph of
$x-y=2$ is the perpendicular bisector of AB
(see Fig. 7.7).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 7.7

blocks.text:
Example 5 : Find a point on the $y$-axis which
is equidistant from the points A(6, 5) and
B$(-4, 3)$.

Solution : We know that a point on the
$y$-axis is of the form $(0, y)$. So, let the point
P(0, $y$) be equidistant from A and B. Then

$$(6 - 0)^2 + (5 - y)^2 = (-4 - 0)^2 + (3 - y)^2$$

i.e., $36 + 25 + y^2 - 10y = 16 + 9 + y^2 - 6y$

i.e., $4y = 36$

i.e., $y = 9$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the required point is $(0, 9)$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let us check our solution : $AP = \sqrt{(6 - 0)^2 + (5 - 9)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 16} = \sqrt{52}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** Using the remark above, we see that $(0, 9)$ is the intersection of the $y$-axis and
the perpendicular bisector of AB.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.3 Section Formula

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us recall the situation in Section 7.2.
Suppose a telephone company wants to
position a relay tower at P between A and B
in such a way that the distance of the tower
from B is twice its distance from A. If P lies
on AB, it will divide AB in the ratio $1 : 2$
(see Fig. 7.9). If we take A as the origin O,
and 1 km as one unit on both the axis, the
coordinates of B will be $(36, 15)$. In order to
know the position of the tower, we must know
the coordinates of P. How do we find these
coordinates?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 7.9

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let the coordinates of P be $(x, y)$. Draw perpendiculars from P and B to the
$x$-axis, meeting it in D and E, respectively. Draw PC perpendicular to BE. Then, by
the AA similarity criterion, studied in Chapter 6, $\Delta$ POD and $\Delta$ BPC are similar.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore , $\frac{\text{OD}}{\text{PC}} = \frac{\text{OP}}{\text{PB}} = \frac{1}{2}$, and $\frac{\text{PD}}{\text{BC}} = \frac{\text{OP}}{\text{PB}} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: These equations give $x = 12$ and $y = 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that $P(12, 5)$ meets the
condition that $OP : PB = 1 : 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now let us use the understanding that
you may have developed through this
example to obtain the general formula.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider any two points $A(x_1, y_1)$ and
$B(x_2, y_2)$ and assume that $P(x, y)$ divides
AB internally in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\frac{\mathrm{PA}}{\mathrm{PB}} = \frac{m_1}{m_2} \text{ (see Fig. 7.10).}$$

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw AR, PS and BT perpendicular to the $x$-axis. Draw AQ and PC parallel to
the $x$-axis. Then, by the AA similarity criterion,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\Delta$ PAQ $\sim \Delta$ BPC

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{PA}}{\mathrm{BP}} = \frac{\mathrm{AQ}}{\mathrm{PC}} = \frac{\mathrm{PQ}}{\mathrm{BC}}$ (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\text{AQ} = \text{RS} = \text{OS} - \text{OR} = x - x_1$
$\text{PC} = \text{ST} = \text{OT} - \text{OS} = x_2 - x$
$\text{PQ} = \text{PS} - \text{QS} = \text{PS} - \text{AR} = y - y_1$
$\text{BC} = \text{BT} - \text{CT} = \text{BT} - \text{PS} = y_2 - y$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting these values in (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Taking $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x}$, we get $x = \frac{m_1 x_2 + m_2 x_1}{m_1 + m_2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, taking $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{y - y_1}{y_2 - y}$, we get $y = \frac{m_1 y_2 + m_2 y_1}{m_1 + m_2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the coordinates of the point P$(x, y)$ which divides the line segment joining the
points A$(x_1, y_1)$ and B$(x_2, y_2)$, internally, in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ are

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is known as the section formula.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This can also be derived by drawing perpendiculars from A, P and B on the
$y$-axis and proceeding as above.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If the ratio in which P divides AB is $k: 1$, then the coordinates of the point P will be

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{kx_2 + x_1}{k+1}, \frac{ky_2 + y_1}{k+1} \right). $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Special Case : The mid-point of a line segment divides the line segment in the ratio
$1 : 1$. Therefore, the coordinates of the mid-point P of the join of the points A($x_1, y_1$)
and B($x_2, y_2$) is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{1 \cdot x_1 + 1 \cdot x_2}{1 + 1}, \frac{1 \cdot y_1 + 1 \cdot y_2}{1 + 1} \right) = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right). $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us solve a few examples based on the section formula.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : Find the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining
the points $(4, -3)$ and $(8, 5)$ in the ratio $3 : 1$ internally.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let $P(x, y)$ be the required point. Using the section formula, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $(7, 3)$ is the required point.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : In what ratio does the point $(-4, 6)$ divide the line segment joining the
points A$(-6, 10)$ and B$(3, -8)$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let $(-4, 6)$ divide AB internally in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$. Using the section
formula, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Recall that if $(x, y) = (a, b)$ then $x = a$ and $y = b$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $-4 = \frac{3m_1 - 6m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ gives us

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: You should verify that the ratio satisfies the $y$-coordinate also.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $$\frac{-8m_1 + 10m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{-8\frac{m_1}{m_2} + 10}{\frac{m_1}{m_2} + 1}$$ (Dividing throughout by $m_2$)

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, the point $(-4, 6)$ divides the line segment joining the points $A(-6, 10)$ and
$B(3, -8)$ in the ratio $2 : 7$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Alternatively : The ratio $m_1 : m_2$ can also be written as $\frac{m_1}{m_2} : 1$, or $k : 1$. Let $(-4, 6)$

divide AB internally in the ratio $k : 1$. Using the section formula, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: You can check for the $y$-coordinate also.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the point $(-4, 6)$ divides the line segment joining the points $A(-6, 10)$ and
$B(3, -8)$ in the ratio $2:7$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** You can also find this ratio by calculating the distances PA and PB and taking
their ratios provided you know that A, P and B are collinear.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 : Find the coordinates of the points of trisection (i.e., points dividing in
three equal parts) of the line segment joining the points A(2, $-2$) and B($-7, 4$).

Solution : Let P and Q be the points of
trisection of AB i.e., AP = PQ = QB
(see Fig. 7.11).

Figure. 7.11

Therefore, P divides AB internally in the ratio 1 : 2. Therefore, the coordinates of P, by
applying the section formula, are

$$\left( \frac{1(-7) + 2(2)}{1 + 2}, \frac{1(4) + 2(-2)}{1 + 2} \right), \text{ i.e., } (-1, 0)$$

Now, Q also divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 1. So, the coordinates of Q are

$$\left( \frac{2(-7) + 1(2)}{2 + 1}, \frac{2(4) + 1(-2)}{2 + 1} \right), \text{ i.e., } (-4, 2)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, the coordinates of the points of trisection of the line segment joining A and
B are $(-1, 0)$ and $(-4, 2)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** We could also have obtained Q by noting that it is the mid-point of PB. So, we
could have obtained its coordinates using the mid-point formula.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 : Find the ratio in which the $y$-axis divides the line segment joining the
points $(5, -6)$ and $(-1, -4)$. Also find the point of intersection.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let the ratio be $k : 1$. Then by the section formula, the coordinates of the

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: point which divides AB in the ratio $k:1$ are $\left(\frac{-k+5}{k+1}, \frac{-4k-6}{k+1}\right)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This point lies on the $y$-axis, and we know that on the $y$-axis the abscissa is $0$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{-k + 5}{k + 1} = 0$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
That is, the ratio is $5 : 1$. Putting the value of $k = 5$, we get the point of intersection as

$$\left( 0, \frac{-13}{3} \right).$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 : If the points A(6, 1), B(8, 2), C(9, 4) and D($p$, 3) are the vertices of a
parallelogram, taken in order, find the value of $p$.

Solution : We know that diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

So, the coordinates of the mid-point of AC = coordinates of the mid-point of BD

i.e., $\left( \frac{6 + 9}{2}, \frac{1 + 4}{2} \right) = \left( \frac{8 + p}{2}, \frac{2 + 3}{2} \right)$

i.e., $\left( \frac{15}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right) = \left( \frac{8 + p}{2}, \frac{5}{2} \right)$

so, $\frac{15}{2} = \frac{8 + p}{2}$

i.e., $p = 7$

A NOTE TO THE READER

Section 7.3 discusses the Section Formula for the coordinates $(x, y)$ of a
point P which divides internally the line segment joining the points
$A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ as follows :

$$x = \frac{m_1x_2 + m_2x_1}{m_1 + m_2} , \quad y = \frac{m_1y_2 + m_2y_1}{m_1 + m_2}$$

Note that, here, $PA : PB = m_1 : m_2$.

However, if P does not lie between A and B but lies on the line AB,
outside the line segment AB, and $PA : PB = m_1 : m_2$, we say that P divides
externally the line segment joining the points A and B. You will study
Section Formula for such case in higher classes.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text:
INTRODUCTION TO
TRIGONOMETRY 8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
There is perhaps nothing which so occupies the
middle position of mathematics as trigonometry.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: - J.F. Herbart (1890)

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already studied about triangles, and in particular, right triangles, in your
earlier classes. Let us take some examples from our surroundings where right triangles
can be imagined to be formed. For instance :

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.1

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Suppose the students of a school are
visiting Qutub Minar. Now, if a student
is looking at the top of the Minar, a right
triangle can be imagined to be made,
as shown in Fig 8.1. Can the student
find out the height of the Minar, without
actually measuring it?

2. Suppose a girl is sitting on the balcony
of her house located on the bank of a
river. She is looking down at a flower
pot placed on a stair of a temple situated
nearby on the other bank of the river.
A right triangle is imagined to be made
in this situation as shown in Fig.8.2. If
you know the height at which the
person is sitting, can you find the width
of the river?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.2

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
3. Suppose a hot air balloon is flying in
the air. A girl happens to spot the
balloon in the sky and runs to her
mother to tell her about it. Her mother
rushes out of the house to look at the
balloon.Now when the girl had spotted
the balloon intially it was at point A.
When both the mother and daughter
came out to see it, it had already
travelled to another point B. Can you
find the altitude of B from the ground?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using
some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called
‘trigonometry’. The word ‘trigonometry’ is derived from the Greek words ‘tri’
(meaning three), ‘gon’ (meaning sides) and ‘metron’ (meaning measure). In fact,
**trigonometry** is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early
astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth.
Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and
Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with
respect to its acute angles, called **trigonometric ratios of the angle**. We will restrict
our discussion to acute angles only. However, these ratios can be extended to other
angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure $0^{\circ}$ and
$90^{\circ}$. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish
some identities involving these ratios, called **trigonometric identities**.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.2 Trigonometric Ratios

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Section 8.1, you have seen some right triangles
imagined to be formed in different situations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown
in Fig. 8.4.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, $\angle$ CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an
acute angle. Note the position of the side BC
with respect to angle A. It faces $\angle$ A. We call it
the \textit{side opposite} to angle A. AC is the
\textit{hypotenuse} of the right triangle and the side AB
is a part of $\angle$ A. So, we call it the \textit{side}
\textit{adjacent} to angle A.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the position of sides change
when you consider angle C in place of A
(see Fig. 8.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied the concept of ‘ratio’ in
your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios
involving the sides of a right triangle, and call
them trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The trigonometric ratios of the angle A
in right triangle ABC (see Fig. 8.4) are defined
as follows :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$sine \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$cosine \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$tangent \ of \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$cosecant \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{1}{sine \text{ of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$secant \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{1}{cosine \text{ of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{AB}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$cotangent \ of \ \angle A = \frac{1}{tangent \ of \ \angle A} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The ratios defined above are abbreviated as $sin A$, $cos A$, $tan A$, $cosec A$, $sec A$
and $cot A$ respectively. Note that the ratios $\boldsymbol{cosec A}$, $\boldsymbol{sec A}$ and $\boldsymbol{cot A}$ are respectively,
the reciprocals of the ratios $sin A$, $cos A$ and $tan A$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, observe that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{\frac{AC}{AB}}{\frac{AC}{AB}} = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ and $\cot A = \frac{\cos A}{\sin A}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the **trigonometric ratios** of an acute angle in a right triangle express the
relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Why don’t you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right
triangle? (See Fig. 8.5)

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
The first use of the idea of ‘$sine$’ in the way we use
it today was in the work $Aryabhatiyam$ by Aryabhata,
in C.E. 500. Aryabhata used the word $ardha-jya$ for
the half-chord, which was shortened to $jya$ or $jiva$ in
due course. When the $Aryabhatiyam$ was translated
into Arabic, the word $jiva$ was retained as it is. The
word $jiva$ was translated into $sinus$, which means
curve, when the Arabic version was translated into
Latin. Soon the word $sinus$, also used as $sine$, became
common in mathematical texts throughout Europe.
An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter
(C.E. 1581–C.E. 1626), first used the abbreviated
notation ‘$sin$’.

The origin of the terms ‘$cosine$’ and ‘$tangent$’ was much later. The cosine function
arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta
called it $kotijya$. The name $cosinus$ originated with Edmund Gunter. In C.E. 1674,
the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation
‘$cos$’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Note that the symbol $sin$ A is used as an
abbreviation for ‘the $sine$ of the angle A’. $sin$ A is
$not$ the product of ‘$sin$’ and A. ‘$sin$’ separated from
A has no meaning. Similarly, $cos$ A is $not$ the product
of ‘$cos$’ and A. Similar interpretations follow for other
trigonometric ratios also.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse
AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle
ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN
perpendicular to AB extended (see Fig. 8.6), how
will the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ PAM differ
from those of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ CAB or from those of $\angle A$ in
$\Delta$ QAN?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To answer this, first look at these triangles. Is $\Delta$ PAM similar to $\Delta$ CAB? From
Chapter 6, recall the AA similarity criterion. Using the criterion, you will see that the
triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles,
the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we have $\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AP}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{\text{MP}}{\text{BC}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From this, we find $$\frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AP}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}} = sin \mathrm{A} .$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, $\frac{\mathrm{AM}}{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}=\cos \mathrm{A}, \frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AM}}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\tan \mathrm{A}$ and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This shows that the trigonometric ratios of angle A in $\Delta$ PAM not differ from
those of angle A in $\Delta$ CAB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the same way, you should check that the value of $sin A$ (and also of other
trigonometric ratios) remains the same in $\Delta$ QAN also.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric
ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if
the angle remains the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** For the sake of convenience, we may write $sin^2A$, $cos^2A$, etc., in place of
$(sin A)^2$, $(cos A)^2$, etc., respectively. But $cosec A = (sin A)^{-1} \neq sin^{-1} A$ (it is called sine
inverse A). $sin^{-1} A$ has a different meaning, which will be discussed in higher classes.
Similar conventions hold for the other trigonometric ratios as well. Sometimes, the
Greek letter $\theta$ (theta) is also used to denote an angle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one
of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in a right triangle ABC, $sin A = \frac{1}{3}$,
then this means that $\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{1}{3}$, i.e., the
lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle
ABC are in the ratio $1:3$ (see Fig. 8.7). So if
BC is equal to $k$, then AC will be $3k$, where
$k$ is any positive number. To determine other
trigonometric ratios for the angle A, we need to find the length of the third side
AB. Do you remember the Pythagoras theorem? Let us use it to determine the
required length AB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AB = \pm 2\sqrt{2}k$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we get $AB = 2\sqrt{2}k$ (Why is AB not $-2\sqrt{2}k$?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}k}{3k} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of
$sin A$ or $cos A$ is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Given $tanA = \frac{4}{3}$, find the other
trigonometric ratios of the angle A.
Solution : Let us first draw a right $\Delta$ ABC
(see Fig 8.8).

Now, we know that $tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{4}{3}$.

Therefore, if $BC = 4k$, then $AB = 3k$, where $k$ is a
positive number.

Now, by using the Pythagoras Theorem, we have

$$AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = (3k)^2 + (4k)^2 = 25k^2$$

So, $$AC = 5k$$

Now, we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions.

$$sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{4k}{5k} = \frac{4}{5}$$

$$cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{3k}{5k} = \frac{3}{5}$$

Therefore, $cot A = \frac{1}{tan A} = \frac{3}{4}$, $cosec A = \frac{1}{sin A} = \frac{5}{4}$ and $sec A = \frac{1}{cos A} = \frac{5}{3}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : If $\angle$ B and $\angle$ Q are
acute angles such that $sin$ B = $sin$ Q,
then prove that $\angle$ B = $\angle$ Q.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us consider two right
triangles ABC and PQR where
$$sin \text{ B } = sin \text{ Q} \text{ (see Fig. 8.9).}$$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.9

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}} = \frac{\mathrm{PR}}{\mathrm{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}}=\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}}=k$, say (1)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, using Pythagoras theorem,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^2 - \mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $QR = \sqrt{PQ^2 - PR^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}} = \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^2 - \mathrm{AC}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{k^2\mathrm{PQ}^2 - k^2\mathrm{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = \frac{k\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = k$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: From (1) and (2), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, by using Theorem 6.4, $\Delta$ ACB $\sim \Delta$ PRQ and therefore, $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{Q}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Consider $\Delta$ ACB, right-angled at C, in
which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and $\angle$ ABC = $\theta$
(see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of
(i) $cos^2 \theta + sin^2 \theta$,
(ii) $cos^2 \theta - sin^2 \theta$.
Solution : In $\Delta$ ACB, we have
$$AC = \sqrt{AB^2 - BC^2} = \sqrt{(29)^2 - (21)^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{(29 - 21)(29 + 21)} = \sqrt{(8)(50)} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{ units}$$
So, $$sin \theta = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{20}{29}, cos \theta = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{21}{29}.$$
Now, (i) $cos^2 \theta + sin^2 \theta = \left( \frac{21}{29} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{20}{29} \right)^2 = \frac{21^2 + 20^2}{29^2} = \frac{441 + 400}{841} = 1$,
and (ii) $cos^2 \theta - sin^2 \theta = \left( \frac{21}{29} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{20}{29} \right)^2 = \frac{(21 + 20)(21 - 20)}{29^2} = \frac{41}{841}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
if $tan A = 1$, then verify that

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$ 2 \sin A \cos A = 1. $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Solution : In $\Delta$ ABC, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = 1$ (see Fig 8.11)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                                                 $BC = AB$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let AB = BC = $k$, where $k$ is a positive number.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\text{AC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2}$

$= \sqrt{(k)^2 + (k)^2} = k\sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\sin A = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \text{and} \quad \cos A = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $2 \sin A \cos A = 2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 1$, which is the required value.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : In $\Delta$ OPQ, right-angled at P,
OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm (see Fig. 8.12).
Determine the values of $sin$ Q and $cos$ Q.

Solution : In $\Delta$ OPQ, we have

$$OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2$$

i.e., $$(1 + PQ)^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$$

i.e., $1 + PQ^2 + 2PQ = OP^2 + PQ^2$

i.e., $1 + 2PQ = 7^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$

i.e., $PQ = 24 \text{ cm and } OQ = 1 + PQ = 25 \text{ cm}$

So, $$sin \text{ Q} = \frac{7}{25} \text{ and } cos \text{ Q} = \frac{24}{25}.$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.3 Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$,
$60^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these
angles and, of course, for $0^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $45^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is $45^{\circ}$, then
the other angle is also $45^{\circ}$, i.e., $\angle A = \angle C = 45^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.14).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\text{BC} = \text{AB} \quad (\text{Why?})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, Suppose BC = AB = $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then by Pythagoras Theorem, $\mathrm{AC}^2 = \mathrm{AB}^2 + \mathrm{BC}^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and, therefore, $AC = a\sqrt{2}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using the definitions of the trigonometric ratios, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$sin 45^\circ = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^\circ}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$cos 45^\circ = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^\circ}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$tan 45^\circ = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^\circ}{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^\circ} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{a} = 1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\cos^0 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sin 45^\circ} = \sqrt{2}$, $\sec 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\cos 45^\circ} = \sqrt{2}$, $\cot 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\tan 45^\circ} = 1$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now calculate the trigonometric ratios of $30^{\circ}$
and $60^{\circ}$. Consider an equilateral triangle ABC. Since
each angle in an equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$, therefore,
$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 60^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw the perpendicular AD from A to the side BC
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now $\Delta ABD \cong \Delta ACD$ (Why?)
Therefore, $BD = DC$
and $\angle BAD = \angle CAD$ (CPCT)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now observe that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\triangle$ ABD is a right triangle, right-angled at D with $\angle$ BAD $= 30^{\circ}$ and $\angle$ ABD $= 60^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you know, for finding the trigonometric ratios, we need to know the lengths of the
sides of the triangle. So, let us suppose that $\text{AB} = 2a$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then, $\text{BD} = \frac{1}{2}\text{BC} = a$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AD = a\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
tive :
$sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}, \cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Also, $\quad cosec \ 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = 2, \ sec \ 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 30^{\circ}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\cot 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 30^{\circ}} = \sqrt{3} .$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Similarly,
$$sin 60^\circ = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3},$$
$$\text{cosec } 60^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \text{sec } 60^\circ = 2 \text{ and } \cot 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of angle
A, if it is made smaller and smaller in the right triangle ABC
(see Fig. 8.16), till it becomes zero. As $\angle$ A gets smaller and
smaller, the length of the side BC decreases.The point C gets
closer to point B, and finally when $\angle$ A becomes very close
to $0^\circ$, AC becomes almost the same as AB (see Fig. 8.17).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, BC gets very close to $0$ and so the value of
$sin A = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}}$ is very close to $0$. Also, when $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, AC is nearly the

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: same as AB and so the value of $cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}$ is very close to 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This helps us to see how we can define the values of $sin$ A and $cos$ A when
$A = 0^\circ$. We define : $sin \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{0}$ and $cos \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{1}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using these, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $tan 0^{\circ} = \frac{sin 0^{\circ}}{cos 0^{\circ}} = 0, cot 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{tan 0^{\circ}},$ which is not defined. (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $sec\ 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{cos\ 0^{\circ}} = 1$ and $cosec\ 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{sin\ 0^{\circ}}$, which is again not defined.(Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$, when it is made
larger and larger in $\Delta ABC$ till it becomes $90^\circ$. As $\angle A$ gets larger and larger, $\angle C$ gets
smaller and smaller. Therefore, as in the case above, the length of the side AB goes on
decreasing. The point A gets closer to point B. Finally when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ becomes very close to $0^\circ$ and the side AC almost coincides with side BC
(see Fig. 8.18).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle C$ is very close to $0^\circ$, $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$, side AC is nearly the
same as side BC, and so $sin A$ is very close to 1. Also when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ is very close to $0^\circ$, and the side AB is nearly zero, so $cos A$ is very close to 0.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we define : $\qquad \sin 90^{\circ} = 1 \text{ and } \cos 90^{\circ} = 0.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, why don’t you find the other trigonometric ratios of $90^\circ$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We shall now give the values of all the trigonometric ratios of $0^{\circ}$, $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$, $60^{\circ}$
and $90^{\circ}$ in Table 8.1, for ready reference.

blocks.label: Table-caption
blocks.text: Table 8.1

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
$\angle A$ $0^\circ$ $30^\circ$ $45^\circ$ $60^\circ$ $90^\circ$
$\sin A$ 0 $\frac{1}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ 1
$\cos A$ 1 $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{1}{2}$ 0
$\tan A$ 0 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1 $\sqrt{3}$ Not defined
$\text{cosec } A$ Not defined 2 $\sqrt{2}$ $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1
$\sec A$ 1 $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sqrt{2}$ 2 Not defined
$\cot A$ Not defined $\sqrt{3}$ 1 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 0

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : From the table above you can observe that as $\angle$ A increases from $0^\circ$ to
$90^\circ$, $sin$ A increases from 0 to 1 and $cos$ A decreases from 1 to 0.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us illustrate the use of the values in the table above through some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B,
AB = 5 cm and $\angle$ ACB = $30^\circ$ (see Fig. 8.19).
Determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC.

Solution : To find the length of the side BC, we will
choose the trigonometric ratio involving BC and the
given side AB. Since BC is the side adjacent to angle
C and AB is the side opposite to angle C, therefore

$$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}} = \tan C$$

i.e., $$\frac{5}{\text{BC}} = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

which gives $$\text{BC} = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To find the length of the side AC, we consider

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} \qquad (\text{Why?})$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                                                    $AC = 10 \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that alternatively we could have used Pythagoras theorem to determine the third
side in the example above,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AC = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} \text{ cm} = 10\text{cm}.$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : In $\Delta$ PQR, right-angled at
Q (see Fig. 8.20), PQ = 3 cm and PR = 6 cm.
Determine $\angle$ QPR and $\angle$ PRQ.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Given PQ = 3 cm and PR = 6 cm.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{PQ}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \sin \mathrm{R}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\sin R = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle PRQ = 30^\circ$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and therefore, $\angle QPR = 60^{\circ}$. (Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may note that if one of the sides and any other part (either an acute angle or any
side) of a right triangle is known, the remaining sides and angles of the triangle can be
determined.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 : If $sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $0^{\circ} < A + B \leq 90^{\circ}$, $A > B$, find A
and B.

Solution : Since, $sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A - B = 30^{\circ}$ (Why?) (1)

Also, since $cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A + B = 60^{\circ}$ (Why?) (2)

Solving (1) and (2), we get : $A = 45^{\circ}$ and $B = 15^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.4 Trigonometric Identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may recall that an equation is called an identity
when it is true for all values of the variables involved.
Similarly, an equation involving trigonometric ratios
of an angle is called a **trigonometric identity**, if it is
true for all values of the angle(s) involved.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we will prove one trigonometric
identity, and use it further to prove other useful
trigonometric identities.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B (see Fig. 8.21), we have:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dividing each term of (1) by $AC^2$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                     $cos^2 \mathbf{A} + sin^2 \mathbf{A} = 1$                                     (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This is true for all A such that $0^{\circ} \leq A \leq 90^{\circ}$. So, this is a trigonometric identity.
Let us now divide (1) by $AB^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $1 + tan^2 \mathbf{A} = sec^2 \mathbf{A}$ (3)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is this equation true for $A = 0^\circ$? Yes, it is. What about $A = 90^\circ$? Well, $tan A$ and
$sec A$ are not defined for $A = 90^\circ$. So, (3) is true for all A such that $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see what we get on dividing (1) by $\text{BC}^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $cot^2 \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{1} = cosec^2 \mathbf{A}$ (4)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that $cosec A$ and $cot A$ are not defined for $A = 0^\circ$. Therefore (4) is true for
all $A$ such that $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using these identities, we can express each trigonometric ratio in terms of other
trigonometric ratios, i.e., if any one of the ratios is known, we can also determine the
values of other trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see how we can do this using these identities. Suppose we know that


$$tan A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \text{ Then, } cot A = \sqrt{3} \text{ .}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Since, $sec^2 A = 1 + tan^2 A = 1 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$, $sec A = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $cos A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Again, $sin A = \sqrt{1-cos^2 A} = \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $cosec A = 2$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 : Express the ratios $cos$ A, $tan$ A and $sec$ A in terms of $sin$ A.

Solution : Since $\quad cos^2 A + sin^2 A = 1$, therefore,

$$cos^2 A = 1 - sin^2 A, \text{ i.e., } cos A = \pm \sqrt{1 - sin^2 A}$$

This gives $\quad cos A = \sqrt{1 - sin^2 A} \quad \text{(Why?)}$

Hence, $\quad tan A = \frac{sin A}{cos A} = \frac{sin A}{\sqrt{1 - sin^2 A}} \text{ and } sec A = \frac{1}{cos A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - sin^2 A}}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 : Prove that $sec A (1 - sin A)(sec A + tan A) = 1$.

Solution :

$$LHS = sec A (1 - sin A)(sec A + tan A) = \left( \frac{1}{cos A} \right) (1 - sin A) \left( \frac{1}{cos A} + \frac{sin A}{cos A} \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ = \frac{(1 - sin \text{ A})(1 + sin \text{ A})}{cos^2 \text{ A}} = \frac{1 - sin^2 \text{ A}}{cos^2 \text{ A}} $$

$$ = \frac{cos^2 \text{ A}}{cos^2 \text{ A}} = 1 = \text{RHS} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 11 : Prove that $\frac{cot \text{ A} - cos \text{ A}}{cot \text{ A} + cos \text{ A}} = \frac{cosec \text{ A} - 1}{cosec \text{ A} + 1}$


Solution : $\text{LHS} = \frac{cot \text{ A} - cos \text{ A}}{cot \text{ A} + cot \text{ A}} = \frac{\frac{cos \text{ A}}{\sin \text{ A}} - cos \text{ A}}{\frac{cos \text{ A}}{\sin \text{ A}} + cos \text{ A}}$


$= \frac{cos \text{ A} \left( \frac{1}{\sin \text{ A}} - 1 \right)}{cos \text{ A} \left( \frac{1}{\sin \text{ A}} + 1 \right)} = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{\sin \text{ A}} - 1 \right)}{\left( \frac{1}{\sin \text{ A}} + 1 \right)} = \frac{cosec \text{ A} - 1}{cosec \text{ A} + 1} = \text{RHS}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 : Prove that $\frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}$, using the identity
$sec^2 \theta = 1 + tan^2 \theta$.

Solution : Since we will apply the identity involving $sec \theta$ and $tan \theta$, let us first
convert the LHS (of the identity we need to prove) in terms of $sec \theta$ and $tan \theta$ by
dividing numerator and denominator by $cos \theta$.

$$LHS = \frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{tan \theta - 1 + sec \theta}{tan \theta + 1 - sec \theta}$$

$$= \frac{(tan \theta + sec \theta) - 1}{(tan \theta - sec \theta) + 1} = \frac{\{(tan \theta + sec \theta) - 1\} (tan \theta - sec \theta)}{\{(tan \theta - sec \theta) + 1\} (tan \theta - sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{(tan^2 \theta - sec^2 \theta) - (tan \theta - sec \theta)}{\{(tan \theta - sec \theta + 1\} (tan \theta - sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{- 1 - tan \theta + sec \theta}{(tan \theta - sec \theta + 1) (tan \theta - sec \theta)}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{-1}{tan \theta - sec \theta} = \frac{1}{sec \theta - tan \theta}, $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the RHS of the identity, we are required to prove.

blocks.text: EXERCISE 8.3

blocks.text:

2. Write all the other trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$ in terms of $sec A$.
3. Choose the correct option. Justify your choice.
(i) $9 sec^2 A - 9 tan^2 A = ...........$
